metadata.name: efs
metadata.overview:
Amazon Elastic File System provides serverless, elastic file storage for Linux-based workloads. It presents a shared POSIX file system that grows and shrinks automatically as files are added and removed, so you do not provision or manage storage capacity. The service manages the underlying file storage infrastructure, including deployment, patching, and configuration.

File systems are accessed over the Network File System protocol, so existing applications and tools work without modification. Many compute clients across multiple Availability Zones can mount the same file system concurrently and share a common data source. On-premises servers can also mount file systems over a private network connection to a virtual private cloud. Regional file systems store data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones, while One Zone file systems keep data in a single Availability Zone.

Access is controlled through a combination of network controls on the file system's mount points, identity and resource policies, and POSIX file and directory permissions. Application-specific entry points can pin a client to a fixed operating system identity and a subdirectory root. Data can be encrypted at rest with managed keys and encrypted in transit when the file system is mounted. Storage lifecycle policies move inactive data to lower-cost tiers, and built-in backup and cross-Region replication support recovery and business continuity objectives.
useCases: Provide a shared POSIX file system that hundreds or thousands of Linux compute clients mount concurrently across multiple Availability Zones, so horizontally scaling applications such as web serving, content management systems, and home directories read and write a single common data source.

Persist and share state for containerized and serverless workloads, giving container tasks and functions durable shared storage that survives task or invocation lifecycles without any capacity provisioning.

Give each application or tenant an isolated slice of one shared file system by pinning it to a fixed operating system user, group, and subdirectory root, so applications cannot read or modify data outside their own directory tree.

Migrate on-premises file data into AWS and support cloud bursting by mounting the same file system from on-premises Linux servers over a private network connection to a virtual private cloud, then analyzing that data on cloud compute fleets.

Meet disaster recovery and business continuity objectives by continuously replicating a file system to another AWS Region or to a separate AWS account, then failing over to the read-only replica and later failing back to the primary.

Cost-optimize long-lived datasets by letting lifecycle policies automatically move inactive files to infrequent access and archive tiers while keeping active data on low-latency storage, and by centralizing scheduled backups with defined retention.

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Core dependency and primary client. Each EFS mount target is backed by a requester-managed EC2 elastic network interface in a VPC subnet, and mount target security groups plus subnet network ACLs are the network access control for NFS port 2049. CreateMountTarget requires ec2:DescribeSubnets, ec2:DescribeNetworkInterfaces and ec2:CreateNetworkInterface; DeleteMountTarget requires ec2:DeleteNetworkInterface; ModifyMountTargetSecurityGroups requires ec2:ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute. EC2 Linux and Mac instances are the primary NFS clients. VPC interface endpoints and AWS Site-to-Site VPN connectivity are also modeled under this namespace.

Encryption-at-rest key management dependency. File data is encrypted with an AWS managed key (aws/elasticfilesystem) or a customer managed symmetric KMS key; EFS requires kms:Decrypt, kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext, kms:CreateGrant and kms:DescribeKey, uses a Forward Access Session for kms:CreateGrant, and passes the file system ID as encryption context. Disabling, deleting, or revoking the grant on the key makes the file system inaccessible.

Authorization dependency. EFS supports identity-based policies, a resource-based file system policy, service-specific condition keys, service roles, and the AWSServiceRoleForAmazonElasticFileSystem service-linked role. NFS clients can authenticate with an IAM role, and cross-account replication requires a customer-created IAM role with an elasticfilesystem.amazonaws.com trust policy plus iam:PassRole.

Audit logging integration. All EFS API calls are recorded as CloudTrail events, and IAM authorization for NFS clients additionally emits NewClientConnection and UpdateClientConnection service events that record the granted client permission set and source IP address. Service-linked role activity appears under AWSServiceRoleForAmazonElasticFileSystem.

Monitoring integration. EFS publishes metrics for throughput, IOPS, client connections, burst credit balance, mount success/failure and replication TimeSinceLastSync, and supports CloudWatch alarms. The EFS managed policies include cloudwatch permissions so the console can render metrics and alarms.

Native backup integration. AWS Backup performs incremental backups and restores of EFS file systems; EFS creates a default backup plan and a default backup vault on the customer's behalf via its service-linked role, and elasticfilesystem:Backup and elasticfilesystem:Restore gate the operations. PutBackupPolicy starts or stops automatic backups.

Data transfer integration. AWS DataSync copies data into and out of EFS file systems, including between two EFS file systems in different AWS Regions or owned by different AWS accounts, and between EFS and NFS/SMB servers, self-managed object storage, Amazon S3, and FSx for Windows File Server.

Data transfer and access integration. AWS Transfer Family exposes EFS file systems over SFTP, FTPS and FTP; the Transfer Family IAM role needs elasticfilesystem:ClientMount and ClientWrite, and EFS blocks cross-account Transfer Family requests when the file system policy is considered public.

Private connectivity option. On-premises Linux servers mount EFS file systems over an AWS Direct Connect connection to the VPC containing the mount targets, enabling data migration, cloud bursting, and backing up on-premises data to EFS.

Compute client integration. Amazon ECS tasks (including AWS Fargate tasks) mount EFS volumes for persistent shared storage; ECS best practice guidance recommends combining mount target security groups, IAM authorization, and EFS access points for task-level access control.
Compute client integration. Amazon EKS pods consume EFS file systems as persistent shared volumes, and EFS is listed as an accessible file storage option for EKS compute.
Compute client integration. AWS Lambda functions can access EFS file systems through the file system interface, typically via an EFS access point, giving serverless functions durable shared state.
Log delivery and data movement. CloudTrail trails deliver EFS API event log files to an Amazon S3 bucket, and AWS DataSync copies data between EFS file systems and S3 buckets.

Configuration recording and compliance. AWS Config records AWS::EFS::FileSystem and AWS::EFS::AccessPoint configuration items, and provides EFS managed rules (for example efs-encrypted-check) and a Security Best Practices for Amazon EFS conformance pack.
Preventive governance. Service control policies in AWS Organizations can enforce EFS encryption requirements across all accounts in an organization.
Client deployment automation. AWS Systems Manager is used to automatically install and manage the amazon-efs-utils EFS client package on EC2 instances.

Credential integration. Requests to the EFS API must be signed with an access key associated with an IAM principal, or with temporary security credentials generated by AWS Security Token Service; NFS clients using IAM authorization present assumed-role credentials.

Related file storage service and DataSync transfer target. AWS DataSync copies data between EFS file systems and FSx for Windows File Server file systems, and FSx is presented alongside EFS as a file storage option for EC2 workloads.
Consumer integration. Amazon SageMaker training jobs can read datasets directly from an EFS file system as one of the supported data input sources.
Tag resolution dependency. The EFS service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForAmazonElasticFileSystem is granted tag:GetResources so EFS can resolve tagged resources on the customer's behalf.

entities.name: AccessPoint
entities.overview:
An Amazon EFS access point is an application-specific entry point into an EFS file system. It applies a fixed operating system user and group, plus a file system path, to every request that arrives through it. Applications connect through the access point instead of mounting the file system root directly.

Access points address two problems in shared file storage. First, they remove reliance on each client asserting its own POSIX user and group identity. The access point substitutes the identity you configure, so ownership and permission checks stay consistent across clients. Second, they confine an application to a chosen subdirectory. Amazon EFS can create that directory for you with the ownership and mode bits you specify.

Each access point has its own identifier, which you can reference in a file system policy. This lets you state which principals may connect through which entry point. Access points suit multi-tenant, containerized, and serverless workloads that share one file system but need separate directory namespaces and identities.

Network reachability and firewall rules remain the responsibility of the file system's mount targets. An access point layers identity and directory scoping on top of that connectivity rather than replacing it.

entities.name: AccountPreference
entities.overview:
Amazon EFS account preferences is an account-level setting, maintained separately in each AWS Region, that controls the identifier format assigned to newly created EFS file systems and mount targets. It selects between the long 17-character identifier format and the legacy short 8-character format.

The setting exists to support the migration to longer resource identifiers. Amazon EFS moved new file systems and mount targets to 17-character identifiers in 2021, and requests to select the short format are now rejected. Identifiers already assigned to existing file systems and mount targets are unchanged by the setting, and a resource keeps its identifier for its lifetime.

Reading the preference lets you confirm which identifier format your account and Region use, which helps when tooling, automation, or downstream systems parse or store EFS resource identifiers in fixed-length fields or pattern matches. The setting holds no file data and no customer content beyond the selected format and the resource classes it applies to.

entities.name: FileSystem
entities.overview:
An Amazon EFS file system is a shared, elastic file store that Linux-based compute resources mount over the NFS protocol. It grows and shrinks automatically as files are added and removed, so no capacity is provisioned in advance. Many clients across Availability Zones can read and write the same data concurrently, which suits shared home directories, content repositories, analytics inputs, and container or serverless workloads that need durable shared state.

Each file system is created as either a Regional store or a One Zone store. Regional file systems keep data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones. One Zone file systems keep data within a single Availability Zone. Performance and throughput settings tune latency and bandwidth for the workload, and storage lifecycle rules move files that are not accessed into lower-cost storage classes and back again.

The file system is also the unit on which protection settings apply. Encryption at rest is selected when the file system is created, and an AWS KMS key protects file contents. A policy attached to the file system controls which principals may mount it, write to it, or act as root, and it can require clients to connect over TLS. Automatic backups and replication to a second file system help meet recovery objectives.

entities.name: MountTarget
entities.overview:
An Amazon EFS mount target is the network entry point through which clients mount an EFS file system. Amazon EFS creates it in a subnet you choose and assigns it a private IP address from that subnet. Clients connect to that address over NFS to read and write file data.

Each mount target lives in a single Availability Zone, and a file system can have one mount target per zone. All of a file system's mount targets reside in one VPC. Clients typically use the file system DNS name, which resolves to the mount target in the client's own Availability Zone. You can request IPv4, IPv6, or dual-stack addressing to match the subnet.

Behind each mount target, Amazon EFS manages an elastic network interface on your behalf. You attach VPC security groups to that interface to control which clients can reach the file system over the NFS port. Those security groups can be replaced later without recreating the mount target. Peered VPCs, transit gateways, and on-premises networks connected through AWS Direct Connect or VPN can also reach a mount target.

mitigations.statement: Amazon EFS service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: Calls to the Amazon EFS API through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink) can target resources outside your organization. Under the resource perimeter objective, your identities can access only trusted resources from your network.

mitigations.statement: Amazon EFS service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: You can call the Amazon EFS API privately from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink. Amazon EFS API calls made over that network path are therefore in scope for the identity perimeter applied on your network.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS access point should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EFS access point is a durable resource that supports its own tags. You can apply tags that describe the owner and purpose of each access point.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system's IAM replication service role should be assumed only by Amazon EFS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: When you replicate an Amazon EFS file system, you can pass an IAM role through `$.Destinations[*].RoleArn` that Amazon EFS assumes to synchronize your data. Restricting this role's trust policy to Amazon EFS, acting on behalf of trusted resources, helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming the role.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should have encryption at rest enabled

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EFS treats encryption at rest as an optional setting that you request through `$.Encrypted` when you create a file system. You cannot encrypt a file system after it is created, so enabling it at creation helps protect your stored file data.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon EFS file system supports a file system policy that EFS evaluates when NFS clients connect. That policy can restrict client access based on the network location a connection originates from.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should have automatic backups enabled

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EFS file system stores durable file data that EFS can capture as restorable recovery points. Amazon EFS provides a native automatic backup setting on the file system itself.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon EFS file system resources

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EFS API calls can target a file system outside your organization, such as the source or destination of a cross-account replication configuration. Restricting those calls to file systems in your organization helps establish a resource perimeter, in which your identities can access only trusted resources.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be protected by an AWS Backup backup plan

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EFS file system stores durable customer file data that AWS Backup can capture in recovery points. AWS Backup natively supports the file system as an independently protectable resource type that a backup plan can target.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be deployed across more than one Availability Zone with the Regional file system type

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EFS lets you choose the file system type when you create a file system, and a Regional file system stores your data redundantly across three or more Availability Zones. A One Zone file system stores data in a single Availability Zone, so it is not resilient to the loss of that Availability Zone.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EFS file system accepts an AWS KMS key identifier through `$.KmsKeyId` to protect its data at rest with a customer managed key. A customer managed key gives you control over the key's lifecycle, audit of its use, and the ability to make your file data unavailable.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should use AWS IAM for NFS client authorization

mitigationContext.context: By default, your file system authorizes NFS clients from the POSIX identity that the client asserts, rather than from IAM. Amazon EFS also supports IAM authorization for the NFS clients that mount your file system.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system's policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: You set the file system policy for your Amazon EFS file system as a complete IAM resource-based policy document through `$.Policy`. When no explicit policy is set, the default policy grants full access to any client that can connect through a mount target.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be replicated to at least one other AWS Region

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EFS can replicate a file system to a service-managed destination file system in another AWS Region. That second copy of your file data helps protect it from a disruption affecting the source Region.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should not allow unauthenticated access through its file system policy

mitigationContext.context: By default, an EFS file system permits clients that connect through a mount target to reach file data without presenting AWS credentials. Requiring authenticated NFS clients is an opt-in choice rather than the default behavior.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EFS file system supports its own IAM resource-based policy, known as the file system policy. That policy determines which accounts and IAM identities, including those in other accounts, are trusted to access the file system.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be configured with a file system policy that requires all connections to be encrypted in transit

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EFS supports resource-based file system policies, evaluated when NFS clients connect. Encryption in transit is selected per connection at mount time, and the service does not require it by default.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon EFS file system is a top-level resource that you can tag at creation and afterward with `TagResource`. Tags let you categorize each file system by owner and purpose.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS file system should be configured to disallow file system policy modifications that would remove all policy-management access for the file system

mitigationContext.context: Your file system carries a resource-based file system policy that governs both policy management and client access to your stored file data. A policy update that removes policy-management access can leave the file system unmanageable and its stored data inaccessible.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS mount target should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: Subnet placement is a required setting on every mount target, carried by `$.SubnetId`. Placing a mount target in a private subnet helps limit which clients can reach your file data.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS mount target should be created in each Availability Zone (AZ) that the file system serves, so that mount target elastic network interfaces (ENIs) exist in more than one AZ

mitigationContext.context: Each mount target is backed by one requester-managed elastic network interface that resides in a single Availability Zone. A file system supports a mount target in each Availability Zone, so multi-zone placement reduces dependence on any one zone.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EFS mount target should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: You attach your own Amazon VPC security groups to a mount target through `$.SecurityGroups[*]`, and those groups act as the virtual firewall controlling which clients can reach your file system over NFS. Omitting them attaches the VPC default security group, so the rule set needs to be chosen deliberately.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make Amazon EFS service API calls

threatContext.context: Amazon EFS supports interface VPC endpoints, so where one is deployed, the `elasticfilesystem` control plane is reachable privately from your VPC network. A principal outside your zone of trust operating from that network can send API requests, signed with its own credentials, against its own resources.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted Amazon EFS resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: Principals in your VPC network can call Amazon EFS API operations against file systems in accounts outside your organization. Calling `CreateReplicationConfiguration` with a cross-account file system ARN in `$.Destinations[*].FileSystemId` can copy your file data to that account.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EFS access point
threats.threatAction: can configure the access point without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An Amazon EFS access point can be created with no tags, or have its existing tags removed later. An untagged access point still works normally and carries no owner or purpose information, so it escapes ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can delete the file system and the file data that the file system contains

threatContext.context: The file system stores your file data, so deleting the resource also removes that data. An IAM principal holding delete permissions can remove the file system through the `DeleteFileSystem` operation, without permissions on individual files.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify a file system policy governing an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can make the file system inaccessible by modifying the file system resource-based policy to deny policy-management and client mount actions for all principals, bypassing the policy lockout safety check

threatContext.context: A principal with `elasticfilesystem:PutFileSystemPolicy` permissions can replace your file system policy with a document that denies policy-management and client mount actions. Bypassing the policy lockout safety check leaves the file system in place but unmanageable, with its stored file data unreachable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete the AWS KMS customer managed key used by an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can delete the AWS KMS customer managed key used by the file system

threatContext.context: Your file system permanently binds a symmetric AWS KMS customer managed key at creation, with no re-key path. A threat actor able to delete that key can render the file system permanently inaccessible without calling any Amazon EFS operation.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify data in an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the file data written to the file system with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: A principal with permissions to create a file system or a replication destination chooses which AWS KMS key encrypts the file data. That key can belong to an account you do not administer.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can configure the file system without required tagging information

threatContext.context: Tagging is optional on a file system and reversible after creation. A file system without the required tags may fall outside your ownership attribution and cost allocation processes.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the file system with an AWS managed KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle

threatContext.context: A principal that can create or modify your Amazon EFS file system can encrypt its file data under the AWS managed key. That key is managed by AWS, so you do not control its permissions, usage scope, or rotation schedule.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public Amazon EFS file systems, or prior knowledge of an existing public file system
threats.threatAction: can access a file system that has been configured to allow public access

threatContext.context: Your file system can be configured to allow public access. A threat actor that enumerates public file systems, or already knows of one, can then access it.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can create the file system to not use encryption at rest

threatContext.context: Encryption at rest is an optional setting on your Amazon EFS file system, chosen when you create it. A principal with permissions to create the file system can leave that setting off, storing file data in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read file data from an Amazon EFS file system where the service uses grant-based KMS authorization
threats.threatAction: can read file data in the file system over the NFS protocol because the KMS key policy cannot restrict which IAM principals can decrypt the data

threatContext.context: Amazon EFS decrypts your file data under a KMS grant it holds, so the key policy cannot restrict which principals read the data. An IAM principal with unintended read permissions and network access to a mount target can read plaintext file data over NFS.
`ClientMount` is used to access file systems in your VPCs with IAM authentication.
`ClientRootAccess` is used to access file systems in your VPCs with IAM authentication.
`ClientWrite` is used to access file systems in your VPCs with IAM authentication.
`PutFileSystemPolicy` allows you to apply a resource-based policy to grant access to a file system. The service currently does not support resource control policies.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted file system, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: Your IAM principals can hold permissions on an untrusted Amazon EFS file system, not only on the file systems you own. Such a principal can send data to that untrusted file system or receive data from it.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can create the file system in a single Availability Zone

threatContext.context: Supplying `$.AvailabilityZoneName` on `CreateFileSystem` creates a One Zone file system that stores your data in exactly one Availability Zone. That file system can have only a single mount target in the same Availability Zone, so an impairment there removes the only path your clients use to reach the data.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on my Amazon EFS file system and access to an unexpected network
threats.threatAction: can interact with my file system from an unexpected network

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions on your file system can interact with it from an unexpected network. That interaction can include mounting the file system over NFS and making Amazon EFS API calls against it.
`ClientMount` is used to access file systems in your VPCs with IAM authentication.
`ClientRootAccess` is used to access file systems in your VPCs with IAM authentication.
`ClientWrite` is used to access file systems in your VPCs with IAM authentication.
`PutFileSystemPolicy` allows you to apply a resource-based policy to grant access to a file system. The service currently does not support resource control policies.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EFS file system that does not require authentication for data plane operations
threats.threatAction: can access the file system without presenting valid credentials

threatContext.context: Your file system exposes an NFSv4 data plane on TCP port 2049 at each mount target, reachable from the local VPC, connected VPCs, and on-premises networks. If a newly created file system grants anonymous clients full access, a client asserting the root user ID of 0 can read, write, and delete any file.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EFS file system through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: can use my file system

threatContext.context: The resource-based policy on your Amazon EFS file system can grant access to an identity outside your organization, deliberately or through an over-broad grant. With network reachability to a mount target, that identity can mount the file system to read, overwrite, or delete your data. It can also copy that data to a file system it owns.
`PutFileSystemPolicy` allows you to apply a resource-based policy to grant access to a file system. The service currently does not support resource control policies.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete files and directories from an Amazon EFS file system
threats.threatAction: can delete files and directories from the file system

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EFS file system stores individually addressable files and directories. An IAM principal with delete permissions can remove them over NFS while the file system itself persists.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EFS file system's IAM replication service role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my replication role and act with its permissions, reading the replicated file system data and creating a replication configuration that targets a destination file system they control

threatContext.context: You author the trust policy on the replication role that your file system's replication configuration designates (`$.Destinations[*].RoleArn`). That policy can name identities outside your organization that can assume the role and replicate your file system's data to a destination they control.

threats.prerequisites: with knowledge of an Amazon EFS file system that has been configured to use client-asserted POSIX UID/GID authentication for NFS clients
threats.threatAction: can take advantage of the weak authentication mechanism to access the file system by mounting it over NFS and asserting an arbitrary UID/GID, including root UID 0

threatContext.context: By default, your file system trusts the numeric POSIX user and group IDs that a mounting NFS client asserts about itself. A threat actor with network reachability to a mount target can mount the file system and claim any identity, including root UID 0.

threats.prerequisites: with permissions to configure AWS network-inspection resources that target the network interfaces used by the Amazon EFS file system in a VPC, or to redirect traffic to or from those interfaces through an inspection appliance they control
threats.threatAction: can capture network traffic at the mount target network interfaces used by the file system or at the redirected path, and read NFS data in transit that has not been encrypted

threatContext.context: Your file system's data plane is reachable only through mount targets in your VPC. Each mount target is a customer-visible elastic network interface that can be named as a flow log, traffic mirror, or route target.

threats.prerequisites: with network adjacency to the connection path between clients and an Amazon EFS file system that has not been configured to encrypt data in transit
threats.threatAction: can capture the file system's NFS network traffic on TCP port 2049 to a mount target elastic network interface and read data in transit that has not been encrypted, including file contents, file names, directory listings and client-asserted POSIX UID and GID values

threatContext.context: A threat actor with network adjacency to the client-to-mount-target path can capture your file system's NFS traffic on TCP port 2049. Captured traffic that is not encrypted reveals file contents, file names, directory listings, and client-asserted POSIX UID and GID values.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon EFS mount target
threats.threatAction: can create the mount target in a single Availability Zone

threatContext.context: An Amazon EFS mount target is a zonal endpoint whose Availability Zone is fixed by the `$.SubnetId` you pass to `CreateMountTarget`, and EFS allows only one mount target per zone. A file system left with a single mount target has one reachable NFS endpoint, so clients lose access to file data if that Availability Zone fails.

threats.prerequisites: who controls a VPC-connected resource in the same VPC as an Amazon EFS mount target
threats.threatAction: can interact with the mount target over NFS on TCP port 2049 through overly permissive network rules and move laterally within the VPC

threatContext.context: Overly permissive inbound network rules on your mount target can admit NFS traffic on TCP port 2049 from any VPC-connected resource. A threat actor controlling such a resource may mount your file system and move laterally within your VPC.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EFS mount target that permits traffic to services and administrative ports from unrestricted sources
threats.threatAction: can reach listening services and administrative ports on the mount target

threatContext.context: An Amazon EFS mount target presents a network interface in your VPC whose inbound security group rules admit traffic to it. An unrestricted source range in those rules lets any host that can route to the interface reach its listening services.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EFS mount target that has been placed in a public subnet
threats.threatAction: can access the mount target directly from an ungoverned network

threatContext.context: A mount target is a VPC network endpoint that NFS clients connect to in order to reach your file system. A mount target placed in a subnet that routes to an internet gateway can be reached directly from an ungoverned network.

threats.prerequisites: with access to an Amazon EFS mount target
threats.threatAction: can submit a volume of NFS requests that exceeds the capacity of the mount target or the network it is connected to

threatContext.context: Your mount target is a network endpoint in your subnet that receives NFS requests and has finite capacity. A threat actor who can reach it can send request volume that exhausts that capacity or the network it connects to.

implementationContext.context: This VPC endpoint policy governs Amazon EFS API calls made through your interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink) with the `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition key. As a result, calls to resources outside your organization are restricted, while exempting AWS services that access resources on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`).

To restrict access to trusted resources, use the `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`, or `aws:ResourceAccount` condition keys. These scope access to resources that belong to a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Use `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` to allow AWS services to use their service principals to send requests from your network. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

guidance.description: Amazon EFS creates a requester-managed elastic network interface for each mount target, in the single subnet you supply. A mount target takes exactly one subnet. Only one mount target is allowed per Availability Zone. Multi-AZ network coverage therefore comes from creating several mount targets, not from a subnet array on one mount target. For a file system that uses Regional storage classes, create a mount target in every Availability Zone from which clients mount the file system. A subnet resides entirely within one Availability Zone, so the subnet you choose fixes the zone. Confirm that your chosen subnet IDs belong to distinct Availability Zones before you create each mount target. Check the `AvailabilityZone` response field of the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so the templates and modules that create mount targets cover more than one Availability Zone. To verify the deployed state, list the file system's mount targets with `DescribeMountTargets`. Each mount target description returns `SubnetId`, `AvailabilityZoneName`, and `NetworkInterfaceId`. You can also enumerate the interfaces with the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation. Confirm that the resulting interfaces span more than one Availability Zone. Spreading mount targets across zones helps keep file system connectivity available when a single Availability Zone is disrupted. A client that reaches the file system only through a mount target in a disrupted zone loses access. To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include the file system in an AWS Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment flags single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Note that a One Zone file system supports only one mount target, which must sit in the file system's own Availability Zone. This recommendation therefore applies to file systems that use Regional storage classes.

guidance.description:
Configure the security groups associated with your mount target following least-privilege best practices. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations, protocols, and ports. Sources and destinations can be IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists. A mount target needs only inbound TCP access on NFS port 2049, from the clients that mount the file system. Where a client is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the client's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. For other clients, use a narrow IP address range or a prefix list rather than an unrestricted address such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. If you omit security groups when you create a mount target, Amazon EFS attaches the VPC default security group. Set them explicitly instead. Use `ModifyMountTargetSecurityGroups` to change the set later. That operation replaces the existing groups rather than merging them.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across an AWS Organization, scoped by account, organizational unit, or tag. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow-list or block-list. It flags non-compliant groups in a central dashboard, notifies you, and can automatically remediate them. A usage audit policy removes unused or redundant groups. Note that Firewall Manager does not update security groups on requester-managed network interfaces, which back your mount targets. Scope content audit policies at the security groups themselves so the rules attached to your mount targets are still audited.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended, such as any path reaching NFS port 2049 from an unrestricted address. Run an analysis with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope` and `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, then review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

managedImplementation.title: Require an Amazon EFS volume to have an automated backup plan
managedImplementation.description: This control checks whether your Amazon EFS file system has been configured with automatic backups through AWS Backup.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) File Systems are protected by a backup plan
managedImplementation.description: Checks if Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) File Systems are protected by a backup plan. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if the EFS File System is not covered by a backup plan.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if a recovery point expires no earlier than after the specified period
managedImplementation.description: Checks if a recovery point expires no earlier than after the specified period. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if the recovery point has a retention point that is less than the required retention period.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) File Systems are in a logically air-gapped vault
managedImplementation.description: Checks if Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) File Systems are in a logically air-gapped vault. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if an Amazon EFS File System is not in a logically air-gapped vault within the specified time period.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if Amazon Elastic File System file systems have tags
managedImplementation.description: Checks if Amazon Elastic File System file systems have tags. Optionally, you can specify tag keys. The rule is NON_COMPLIANT if there are no tags or if the specified tag keys are not present. The rule does not check for tags starting with 'aws:'.

managedImplementation.title: Checks if an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) mount target is not associated with a public subnet
managedImplementation.description: Checks if an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) mount target is not associated with a public subnet. The rule is NON-COMPLIANT if the Amazon EFS mount target is associated with a public subnet.
